en: The Sūtra on the Distinction Between Good and Evil as They Arise, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. Then the Buddha felt deep compassion.

Because there are all manner of beings subject to birth and death, the karmic destinies are manifested to distinguish between good and evil; in total, there are five paths. Humans perform good and evil in varying degrees, and their anger varies in intensity. The Way of Heaven shows no partiality, but always favors the virtuous. What are these five paths?
First is the path of devas; second is the path of humans; third is the path of hungry ghosts; fourth is the path of animals; fifth is the path of the hells, such as Niraya and Mount Tai.

Those who do not seek the path that leads beyond the world will not sever the cycle of birth, death, sorrow, and suffering; they will continue to wander through the five realms of existence and fail to attain liberation.

The wise and discerning person grows weary of sorrow and suffering; when they see their teacher, they serve them, and when they do not see them, they reflect upon the teacher’s instructions and admonitions.
The Master teaches people to abandon evil and embrace goodness, showing them the Way to transcend the world.
Parents raise and nurture us for but a single lifetime—ending in old age, sickness, and death—whereas the Buddha delivers beings for ten thousand ages without end.
Wise and sagacious persons should reflect upon this thoroughly.
The Buddha addressed his disciples: "Listen all!"
"I shall explain for you the calamities and blessings of good and evil.
All the disciples knelt with their hands joined in reverence and said, "Yes!"
"I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said:
"If a person in this world maintains a mind of loving-kindness and refrains from killing, they will obtain five blessings as a result of that non-killing."
What are the five?
First, the increase of lifespan;
second, physical well-being and security.
Third, one will not be harmed by weapons, tigers, wolves, or venomous insects;
fourth, one will attain rebirth in heaven, where the lifespan is infinite;
fifth, when descending from heaven to be born into the human world, one will possess longevity.
Now we see those who have reached a hundred years of age; all this is brought about by their non-killing in past lives.
To die in happiness is better than to live in suffering—this is clear and distinct; be careful not to commit killing.
The Buddha said:

"If a person does not take the property of others in this world, does not pick up what has been left behind on the road, and their mind is not greedy for profit, they will thereby obtain five virtues."
What are the five?
First, one's wealth and goods increase daily;
second, they are not lost or left behind.
Third, they possess fearlessness;
fourth, they attain rebirth in the heavens where there are many rare treasures;
fifth, when descending from the heavens to be born into the human world, they preserve their wealth and property, which neither government officials nor thieves dare to seize or violate.
Those who currently possess wealth until they reach old age have all done so because, in their past lives, they did not dare to take the property of others.
Whether one's loss is great or small, it causes people anxiety and distress.
"It is better to preserve what one possesses than to lose it; this is clearly so—be careful never to take the property of others!
The Buddha said:
"If a person in this world does not violate the wives of others and does not harbor depraved thoughts, they shall obtain five benefits from this."
What are the five?
First, not wasting or squandering;
second, not fearing the local authorities; [and so forth].
Third, one does not fear people;
fourth, one attains rebirth in heaven, where celestial jade maidens serve as wives;
fifth, when descending from heaven to be born into the human world, one has many beautiful wives.
"Now, Venerable One, you see that these various wives of yours, beautiful and of fine countenance, have all attained this as a result of not violating the wives of others in their past lives.
This is clearly evident before your eyes; be careful not to violate the wives of others!"
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world does not engage in divisive speech to slander others, does not use harsh language to revile others, and does not speak falsehoods or frivolous words, they will thereby obtain five virtues."
What are the five?
First, their words are all trusted;
second, they are loved by others.
Third, the breath from one's mouth is fragrant and pleasant;
fourth, one attains rebirth in the heavens and is revered by the devas;
fifth, when descending from the heavens to be born into the human world, one possesses fine teeth and gums, such that others do not dare to defile them with harsh speech.
Now, those whom we see today who have not been slandered from birth until old age all owe this to the virtuous speech they guarded with their mouths in their past lives.
This is clearly evident; be careful never to slander others falsely!
The Buddha said:
"If a person does not drink intoxicants and become drunk in this world, they obtain five benefits from such sobriety.
What are these five? "
First, when conveying messages or appearing before officials, one’s speech shall be free from error, and one’s official career shall proceed according to one's wishes;
second, one’s household affairs shall be well-managed, and there shall always be surplus wealth;
third, one shall quickly obtain profit from loans and investments, and shall be respected and loved by others.
Fourth, one attains rebirth in the heavens and is likewise revered by the devas;

fifth, descending from the heavens to be born into the human world, one is pure and self-joyful, possessing wisdom and an understanding of affairs—all of which results from the fact that in one's past lives one did not drink alcohol.
"Be careful not to drink alcohol!
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world does not carry weapons or staves to intimidate others, does not inflict pain upon others with their hands or feet, does not incite strife or cause separation among people, and does not impose upon others what they themselves do not desire, they will thereby obtain five virtues."
What are the five?
First, the body is strong and healthy;
second, one is always peaceful and secure when lying down or rising.
Third, one will be protected and watched over by devas, nāgas, and spirits;
fourth, one will attain rebirth in the heavens, where celestial bliss is infinite;
fifth, when descending from the heavens to be born again in the world, one’s body will be complete and free from disease.
Now we see those who, from birth until old age, have never suffered from illness; these are all the result of not inflicting pain upon others in their past lives.
This is clearly evident; therefore, be careful not to inflict evil upon others!
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world maintains a harmonious mind and is free from anger, honoring the worthy when they see them and practicing patience toward the foolish, they shall thereby obtain five benefits."
What are the five?
First, one is praised by others;
second, all who see one feel joy.
Third, one’s own body shall be peaceful, secure, and well-nourished;
fourth, one shall attain rebirth in the heavens, where one will be upright, pure, and clean;
fifth, descending from the heavens to be born into the human world, one will possess a virtuous nature and be upright, beautiful, and excellent.

Now we see those who are excellent people, chosen from among ten thousand, all of whom have attained this through their harmonious minds, virtuous natures, and practice of forbearance in past lives and karmic destinies.
They are free from anger; this is clearly evident. Therefore, be careful never to harbor anger toward others!
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world is filial and obedient toward their parents, respectfully serves their elders, maintains a humble and reverent demeanor, kneels first and rises last, speaks last and remains silent first, and constantly teaches those who do evil to perform good deeds, they shall thereby obtain five virtues."
What are the five?
First, one is respected and loved by others;
second, all people speak of one's virtues.
Third, one’s own mind is filled with joy;
fourth, one attains rebirth in the heavens and is revered and loved by the devas;
fifth, descending from the heavens to be born into the human world, one is cherished and beloved by the masses.

That we now see those who possess a virtuous mind and are filial, and who are thus cherished and loved by the multitude, is entirely due to their practice of filiality and respectful service toward their elders in previous lives.
"In this way, being clearly discerning, one may perform acts of filial piety toward one's elders!
The Buddha said:

"When a person in this world uses admonition and instruction with a virtuous mind and good intentions, serving their elders with reverence and being fully endowed with ritual propriety, they thereby obtain five benefits."
What are the five?
First, those in government service obtain excellent positions;
second, those in office are rapidly promoted, and those who trade gain profit.
Third, when the common people see him, they all rejoice;
fourth, when he ascends to heaven, the various devas who see him all rejoice;

fifth, descending from heaven to be born into the world, he becomes the son of kings, lords, dukes, or high ministers—all of which is brought about by the practice of propriety and the cultivation of merit in his former lives.
"Be thus clearly aware; take care not to be arrogant toward others!
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world is not stingy or greedy, delights in giving alms, and looks with love upon the poor among their own family and relatives, as well as beggars—always ensuring they have sufficient food and drink and that their clothing is complete and intact—they shall thereby obtain five benefits."
What are the five?
First, one's wealth and property increase daily;
second, one is praised by all people throughout the world.
Third, they will be respected by the prefectures, commanderies, and kingdoms;
fourth, they will ascend to heaven and be attended upon there;

fifth, when descending from heaven to be born into the world, they will possess great wealth and happiness and be revered by the multitude—all of which results from the practice of charity and the performance of good deeds in their past lives.
"One who is thus clearly discerning may also practice virtue and give alms!
The Buddha said:

"In this world, there are those who are wise and learned in the scriptures, such as śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way. If one delights in going to them to inquire about the path to transcendence, and with a mind free from jealousy and greed, cherishes these noble and far-reaching sages, one shall thereby obtain five benefits."
What are the five?
First, attaining wisdom;
second, being well-learned, as well as possessing extensive knowledge and vision.
Third, they will be greatly respected and revered;
fourth, they will attain rebirth in the heavens, where they shall recognize what they have learned;

fifth, when descending from the heavens to be born into the world, they will immediately understand the scriptures and be enlightened regarding the Way, being held in high esteem by the state and looked up to as a model by all people.

That we now see those who clearly understand the scriptures and are enlightened regarding the Way—all this is brought about by the practice of the Way and the cultivation of virtue in their past lives.
Since this is so evident, one may likewise practice the Way and cultivate virtue!
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the disciples were filled with joy and came forward to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Listen to how the commission of evil brings about suffering!"
All the disciples joined their palms and said,
"Yes! We accept the Buddha's teaching!"
The Buddha said:
"If a person in this world delights in killing and lacks a heart of compassion, they will obtain five evils from this.
What are the five?
First, their lifespan is short;
second, they experience much fear and terror;
third, they have many enemies and grudges.

Fourth, after ten thousand generations, their souls and spirits shall enter the Tai Shan hell—within the Tai Shan hell, they are subjected to agonizing torture, being burned, roasted, steamed, and boiled; they are hacked, pierced, butchered, and flayed; their entrails are crushed and their bones broken, such that they long for life but cannot attain it. Because they committed the great sin of killing, they remain there for a very long time before finally emerging.

Fifth, when they emerge from the hell and are reborn as humans, they will always be short-lived: some die while still in the womb, some die upon birth, some die within dozens of days or hundreds of days, and others die at the age of dozens of years.

Now we see those who have short lifespans, or whose bodies bear scars and sores, whose limbs are incomplete, or who are lame, hunchbacked, or deformed; or those who are blind, deaf, mute, or suffer from nasal congestion and catarrh; or those who lack hands or feet, or whose bodily orifices are blocked—all of these result from having engaged in slaughter, hunting, netting, or fishing in past lives, and from cruelly killing mosquitoes, gadflies, turtles, tortoises, fleas, and lice.
"Be thus clearly aware; take care not to commit killing! The Buddha said:

"In this world, if a person steals or robs others, forcibly seizing the property of others, seeking profit through improper means, or taking wealth through fraud; if they deceive people with light scales, small measures, or short rulers; or if they encroach upon others with heavy scales, large measures, or long rulers; if they pick up lost items on the road and take what does not belong to them; if they fail to repay debts or loans; or if they act with hostility toward others—by these acts, one incurs five evils."
What are the five?
First, one's wealth and possessions diminish day by day;
second, one is pursued by the laws of the king, and upon realizing one is to be punished, few escape.
Third, if one’s body has never found peace or refuge, one constantly harbors fear and deceives oneself;
fourth, after death, the soul enters the Mount Tai hell—where within the Mount Tai hell, one undergoes millions of forms of torment and punishment—receiving retribution according to one's deeds;

fifth, upon emerging from the hell, one must repay debts according to their lightness or gravity: some must repay as slaves, some as oxen, horses, mules, donkeys, or camels, and some as pigs, sheep, geese, ducks, chickens, or dogs—all such birds, beasts, fish, and turtles are those who are burdened by debt.
As the Sūtra says:
"A debt does not rot. This is precisely what is meant!
We see now that those belonging to the lowly class of animals are all the result of having greedily sought profit and forcibly seized the wealth and property of others during their past lives.
"The sufferings of animals are thus clearly evident before our eyes; be careful not to take the property of others!
The Buddha said:
"When a person in this world commits adultery with the wives of others, they will incur five evils as a result."
What are the five?
First, the household is disharmonious; husband and wife frequently quarrel, and wealth and property are repeatedly lost.

Second, they fear the local officials and are constantly subjected to beatings and staffs; they are objects of the king’s law, their bodies must endure punishment, and there are many deaths with few survivors.
Third, they deceive themselves and are constantly terrified of others;

fourth, they enter the Tai Shan hell—within the Tai Shan hell, an iron pillar is glowing bright red and they must constantly embrace it, receiving this retribution because they committed adultery with the wives of others—and only after such a period of many tens of millions of years does their physical form finally perish;

fifth, upon emerging from the hell, they are reborn as chickens, wild ducks, birds, domestic ducks, or humans, for their souls and spirits have no fixed form and that which they inhabit is merely a name.
Now we see that chickens and ducks are lustful and lewd, not avoiding even their own mothers and children, and lacking all restraint.

Yet there are also the constancy of dogs and horses; the dog is faithful to its master, and among the species of animals, all possess sufficient integrity. Yet chickens and ducks alone are lustful and lack any sense of moderation. This is because in their past lives, they were lustful and violated the wives of others; having received this body of a chicken or duck as retribution, they must now be devoured by people.
"Such diligent suffering is beyond words.
Thus clearly understood, take care never to violate the wives of others!
The Buddha said:

"In this world, people delight in divisive speech and slandering others; they delight in harsh words, false speech, and frivolous chatter; they are self-conceited, revile the noble path, envy the virtuous and the capable, and disparage those of high talent; from these, they incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, having many enemies and those one hates;
second, deceiving oneself, and furthermore, being distrusted by all people.
Third, they frequently encounter misfortunes;

fourth, they enter the Great Mountain Hell—within the Great Mountain Hell, there are spirits who pull out their tongues from the nape of their necks, or hook their tongues with glowing iron hooks until they are severed, or pierce their throats with glowing iron awls; they neither die nor can they live, and are unable to speak, remaining in this state for many tens of millions of years;

fifth, when they emerge from the hell and become human again, they are foul-mouthed, their teeth may be missing or decayed, they may have stiff tendons, be lame or stammer, or be mute and unable to speak.
Now we see that these people are all those who, in their past lives, were double-tongued slanderers who defamed the Holy Path; this is clearly the result of such actions.
Since this is so evident, one should likewise be cautious regarding harsh speech!
The Buddha said:
"When people in this world take pleasure in drinking alcohol and become intoxicated, they incur thirty-six losses.
What are these thirty-six losses?

First, when people drink wine and become intoxicated, they cause their sons not to respect their parents and their ministers not to respect their sovereign; thus, among sovereigns and ministers, fathers and sons, there is no distinction of superior and subordinate.
Second, their speech becomes frequently confused and erroneous.
Third, once intoxicated, they engage in double-tongued talk and excessive gossip.
Fourth, when people have hidden or private matters, they speak of them while intoxicated;
fifth, being drunk, they revile Heaven and urinate upon the altar of the local deity, showing no regard for taboos or prohibitions;
sixth, they lie down in the middle of the road, unable to return home, or lose their personal belongings.
Seventh, when intoxicated, one is unable to correct oneself;
eighth, when intoxicated, one walks unsteadily with head bowed or tilted, or falls into ditches and pits;
ninth, when intoxicated, one stumbles and collapses, and upon rising again, breaks or injures one's face and eyes.
Tenth, errors and delusions in buying and selling, and recklessly causing injury or offense;
eleventh, losing one's sense of duty when intoxicated and showing no concern for managing one's livelihood;
twelfth, the depletion and reduction of all one's wealth and possessions.
Thirteenth, when intoxicated, one no longer thinks of one's wife and children or their hunger and cold;
fourteenth, when intoxicated, one shouts and reviles others without avoiding the laws of the king;
fifteenth, when intoxicated, one strips off one's clothes and drawers, running about naked.
Sixteenth, when intoxicated, they will recklessly enter people's homes, seize their women and children, and engage in disruptive speech; their transgressions are beyond measure.
Seventeenth, when someone passes by, they desire to fight with them.
Eighteenth, they trample the ground and shout aloud, startling and disturbing their neighbors.
Nineteenth, when intoxicated, one recklessly kills insects and small creatures;
twentieth, when intoxicated, one beats those in the house and breaks the household goods;
twenty-first, when intoxicated, the family members regard one as a drunken prisoner, and one speaks words that burst forth impulsively from the mouth.
Twenty-second, associating with wicked people;
twenty-third, distancing oneself from the virtuous and good;
twenty-fourth, when awakening from sleep after being intoxicated, the body feels as if it were afflicted by illness.
Twenty-fifth, when intoxicated, one vomits as if expelling foul secretions, and even one's wife and children loathe their appearance;
twenty-sixth, when intoxicated, one’s mind becomes wanton and dissolute, like an elephant or a wolf that knows no bounds of avoidance;
twenty-seventh, when intoxicated, one fails to respect those who have mastered the scriptures and the wise, nor does one respect the Daoist masters or the śramaṇas.
Twenty-eighth, when intoxicated, one becomes lewd and licentious, having no sense of fear or avoidance;
twenty-ninth, when intoxicated, one becomes like a madman, and all who see him flee;
thirtieth, when intoxicated, one becomes like a dead person, possessing no further consciousness or cognition.
Thirty-first, one may become intoxicated and develop a blotched face, or contract alcohol-related illnesses until one becomes utterly withered and jaundiced;
thirty-second, devas, nāgas, and spirits all regard alcohol as evil;
thirty-third, one’s close relatives and intimate friends distance themselves from one day by day.
Thirty-fourth: when intoxicated, he will squat and glare at officials; perhaps he will be subjected to flogging and have both eyes gouged out. Thirty-fifth:

after ten thousand lifetimes, he shall enter the Tai Shan Hell, where molten copper is constantly poured into his mouth, burning through his belly and passing out below; thus, for thousands of millions of years, it will be difficult for him to seek life and difficult to seek death.
Thirty-sixth: having emerged from the hell, if he is reborn as a human, he will always be dull-witted and ignorant of all things.
Now we see that those who are foolish and lack discernment are all the result of having delighted in wine during their past lives.
This is clearly evident; one should therefore be cautious regarding alcohol!
"Alcohol has thirty-six faults; whoever drinks alcohol commits all thirty-six faults.
The Buddha said:

"In this world, people delight in wielding staves to intimidate others, inflicting pain upon others with their hands and feet, delighting in quarreling and causing the separation of people, and forcibly imposing upon others what they themselves do not like; from these, one incurs five evils."
What are the five?
First, one deceives oneself and becomes a source of affliction and poison to others;
second, one’s body becomes a cause of terror.
Third, they will frequently suffer from illness;
fourth, upon entering the Tai Shan mountains and the hells, they will undergo punishment according to their deeds for ten thousand years;
fifth, after emerging from hell, they will be born as humans who are often ill and never free from the use of a staff.

Now we see that those who suffer from many ailments are all the result of their fondness for inflicting pain and disease upon others in their past lives; having many illnesses is not as good as being strong and healthy.
This is clearly evident; therefore, be careful never to inflict evil upon others!
The Buddha said:

"In this world, people constantly delight in anger and lack harmony; they become angry upon seeing the virtuous and likewise angry upon seeing the foolish. They do not distinguish between good and evil, desiring only to harbor anger, and from this they incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, one burns one's own body;
second, one also disturbs one's own mind.
Third, they will experience restlessness while lying down or rising, or may commit suicide out of grief and anger;
fourth, they will enter the Tai Shan hell, where they will undergo agonizing torture for tens of millions of years;
fifth, upon emerging from the Tai Shan hell, they will be reborn as humans with constantly hideous faces, their complexions withered, black, yellow, or parched.

Now, those seen who possess an ugly complexion are all the result of their delight in anger during their past lives; their faces are of an unseemly and foul appearance, unlike that of a handsome and upright countenance.
"This being so clear, take care not to give way to anger!
The Buddha said:

"If a person in this world is unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their elders, and upon seeing others who are filial to their parents and respectful in serving their elders, constantly harbors anger toward them and takes no pleasure in performing good deeds, they will thereby incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, one constantly has bad dreams;
second, one is detested by others.
Third, one acquires an evil reputation;
fourth, one enters the Tai Shan hell to undergo interrogation and punishment for tens of millions of years;
fifth, upon emerging from the hell and being reborn as a human, one possesses a base nature that is not pleasing, and is loathed by all people.

Now, those who are seen to be fickle and impatient, and who are detested by the multitude, all result from their failure in past lives to be filial toward their parents and respectful toward their elders.
"This is clearly so; be careful not to be arrogant!
You must be filial and obedient, and serve the elders with respect.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"If people in this world are unfilial toward their elders, lack propriety and ritual, are frivolous and arrogant, and act with self-will and obstinacy, they will thereby incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, the loss of one’s position;
second, deceiving oneself.
Third, one will not be respected by others;
fourth, one will enter the Tai Shan hell to undergo interrogation and punishment for many tens of millions of years;
fifth, upon emerging from the hell and being reborn as a human, one will be lowly, base, and ugly, and will be treated with contempt by others.
Now we see that those who are lowly and base in this life all result from arrogance and a lack of respect for their elders in their past lives.
This is clearly evident; therefore, be careful not to be arrogant!
The Buddha said:

"If a person acquires wealth and property in this world, yet out of stinginess and greed refuses to practice giving; if they do not look with affection upon the poor and destitute of their own households and fail to provide for them; if they do not serve śramaṇas or learned practitioners of the Way; if they neither beg nor give to beggars; and if, when there is food and drink for the sick, they do not dare to satisfy themselves, nor dare to wear complete clothing and bedding—through these actions, they shall incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, one deceives oneself and is likewise not respected by others;
second, everyone calls one a "money-guarding slave."
Third, they are constantly burdened by shame and remorse.

Fourth, when they fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), their suffering is beyond description; for a thousand or a hundred years, they cannot obtain water to drink. Even if they see rivers, lakes, or the waters of mountain torrents from afar and run toward them to drink, the water instantly transforms into molten copper or pus and blood, making it undrinkable.

Such intense suffering cannot be fully recounted. Fifth, when they emerge from among the hungry ghosts and are born as humans, they shall be poor and starved; with their vertebrae supporting one another, they beg for alms but receive nothing, and people will spit upon and revile them.
The poor beggars seen today are all the result of their stinginess and greed in past lives, which led them to refuse to practice giving.
This is clearly evident; therefore, be careful not to be stingy or greedy!
The Buddha said:

"If there are in this world those who are learned in the scriptures and wise—such as śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way—and one does not take pleasure in going to them to inquire about the path to transcendence, but instead envies their superior talent and slanders the wise, one will thereby incur five evils."
What are the five?
First, lack of wisdom;
second, meager knowledge;
Third, one will not be respected by others;
fourth, one will enter the Tai Shan Hell—having entered the Tai Shan Hell, one will undergo interrogation and punishment for tens of millions of years;
fifth, upon emerging from the hell, one will be born as a human who is foolish and ignorant, no different from the beasts.

Those seen today who are foolish and unable to distinguish between white and black are all the result of their past lives, wherein they took no delight in the Way and its Virtue and were driven by envy toward those who were lofty and far-reaching.
"Thus it is clearly evident; be careful as you practice the Path!
The Buddha said:
"When a person seeks long life, they obtain long life; when they do not seek long life, they do not obtain long life."
If one seeks illness, one obtains illness; if one does not seek illness, one does not obtain illness.
If one seeks a handsome appearance and fair complexion, one obtains a handsome appearance and fair complexion;
if one seeks an ugly appearance and dark complexion, one obtains an ugly appearance and dark complexion.
If one seeks favor, one obtains favor; if one does not seek favor, one does not obtain favor.
If one seeks lowliness, one obtains lowliness; if one seeks wealth, one obtains wealth; if one seeks poverty, one obtains poverty.
If one seeks to master the scriptures and understand the Way, one masters the scriptures and understands the Way; if one seeks folly, one obtains folly.
When a person performs good, they obtain good; through various merits, they ascend to heaven, or if born as a human, they attain nobility and honor, and are also endowed with physical beauty.
If a person commits evil, they obtain evil; through various transgressions, they may enter the Mount Tai hell, or fall among the hungry ghosts, or fall among the animals.
Even if they should happen to become a human, they will be lowly and base, impoverished, lacking in knowledge and understanding, and moreover, possessed of an ugly appearance.
It is like a person who plants bitter seeds and harvests bitter fruit, or plants sweet seeds and harvests sweet fruit.

To illustrate this with the metaphor of planting the five grains: plant rice and you harvest rice; plant beans and you harvest beans. Likewise, when a person performs good deeds they obtain good results, and when they perform evil deeds they obtain evil results!
One who transmits afar and is far-reaching must guard against excessive scrutiny; one who is deeply faithful and maintains singleness of mind must guard against obstruction and concealment;
one who is courageous, fierce, and resolute must guard against violence and disorder; one who is benevolent, loving, gentle, and kind must guard against lack of continuity;
one whose mind is broad and vast must guard against doubt and suspicion; and one who is profound, pure, peaceful, and relaxed must guard against procrastination.
Carving and chiseling are excessive when done in haste; one must guard against being fickle and impetuous. When many people offer long-winded farewells, one must guard against insincerity.
Let the worthy person maintain these precepts; practicing them brings three kinds of goodness:
one is honored by many, the foolish seek much, and at the end of life, one receives a celestial body.

Abiding in the practice of the precepts to their full extent, having used wisdom to restrain the activities of the mind, one will surely reach the destination reached by such practice and completely sever all that is to be experienced.
Through the precepts, suffering may be extinguished; the precepts stand supreme throughout the three times.
He subdues the dragons of evil poison, so that they do not offend those who possess the precepts.
Excellent is the one honored for their precepts; through faith, they may be taken as companions.
This path is not of ordinary speech; therefore, it is called the Honored One of Precepts.
The noble precepts are a worthy refuge; at the end of life, one’s body shall not be burned.
Having lain down at night in peace, one awakens from sleep with joy.
Honored and respected by the multitude, one uses strength for the sake of one's own well-being.
Regarding the Dharma, I see myself as supreme; having renounced the world, I am the Heavenly King.
I am the uniquely honored one in the world; I have already escaped the afflictions of the world.
Throughout all realms of humans and devas, even as I compare myself to the armies of Māra.
Only the Buddha has undergone diligent hardships, numbering as many as the kalpas that cannot be counted;
though he has traversed the five realms of existence, he has not yet fully unraveled the threads [of karma].
When the wicked conceal their gains, they cry out and expose his shortcomings.
Those who worship the Buddha today, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, shall attain heaven through this worship and achieve long life among humans.
The Buddha is the most honored and supreme awakened one; he has manifested the perfection of wisdom.
The current assembly of those who observe the rites and laws possesses virtues as vast as the ocean and rivers.
Therefore, I shall expound the sacred scriptures of the Buddha,
concerning the causal origins from the beginning and the good and evil of one’s conduct.
Extensively gathered and composed, following the essential meanings of the sūtras, I have compiled this narrative as the Buddha himself pointed it out: the deeds that bring about calamity or merit.
Having already awakened to the Dharma by himself, Brahmā and Śakra descended to request [its teaching].
The World-Honored One has abridged the scriptural teachings; their essential points are difficult to perceive or hear.
Suffering arises from the causes and conditions of suffering; when suffering is exhausted, one becomes a World-Honored One.
By practicing the Eightfold Path as it should be, the extinction of suffering constitutes purity.
From volitional formations arise the fruits of suffering; this was taught by the Hero among Men.
This is fundamentally rooted in the mind; from it, the activities of labor arise.
That which brings about the cessation and healing of all these labors is the sublime essence of practice.
Therefore, I have explained this in due order; it is truly as the Great Holy Honored One has taught.
Thus, I have composed this scripture to provide a model for the world to observe;
it accords with what is correct and is free from doubt, and is that which the wise should adopt.
Nor is it created by a deity, which would render misfortune and fortune devoid of cause;
nor is it the spontaneous nature of things, nor can it be transmitted by time.
If it were in heaven, how could it be without cause? The same applies to time and nature.
Whether superior or inferior, their reality is not without action.
From delusion comes toil; this toil arises from action.
Having acted, one passes beyond even liberation; listen to this, for it is not for those of a single class.
I have compiled the subtle purport of the sutras and the various essentials of the Vinaya;
thus one may fully understand the origins of the world, with each section clearly distinguished.
Through spiritual liberation, I have resolved doubts and manifested the sutras within this world.
Virtuous conduct brings a reward of merit; one should not fail to recognize this.
Having committed unrighteous deeds, at death one falls into the evil realms.
Immediately upon seeing King Yama, the King takes pity and binds him fast:
"Infants, the aged, and the dead—admonish them that they shall face punishment;
knowing there are these five messengers, why do you not cultivate virtue?
Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, only precepts and generosity are supreme."
"What is your intention alone, that you can refrain from doing good?
At that time, there was a criminal who, hearing the king’s admonition according to the Dharma, reflected upon his own lack of virtuous conduct; filled with fear, he entered and replied:
"Only because you associate with evil friends, And hear the common, unrighteous words, And sit [in heedlessness] due to greed and corruption, You are unable to cultivate virtue and goodness.
The King said: 'A human life is difficult to obtain; Having fortunately attained it, why do you not do good?'"
What is so difficult for your nature to awaken to, that you create the karma of the hells?
Since you originally gave rise to this evil, it was not caused by your parents;
it was not the work of śramaṇas or Daoists, nor was it the fault of your sovereign or my teaching.
With a mind of delusion and complacency, one commits these unwholesome deeds;
what one has done oneself, one must now receive the retribution for.
Though instructed by the five messengers with words of loyalty and rectitude, [one does not heed them].
Thereupon, King Yama, the Lord of Dharma, remained silent and did not speak with him.
Only then was the sinner recorded and placed within the realm of Yama;
being led away by the neck into hell, he saw the horrors and became utterly terrified.
First entering the Black Rope Hell, they all cry out together, great and small;
next entering the Avīci Hell, blazing fires consume their forms.
Treading upon thorns and planting feet on hot earth, they traverse directly through boiling ash and water.
The Iron Hells number sixteen in all, extending as far as the Sword-Leaf Trees.
Because people commit evil deeds, these nirayas were brought into existence;
therefore, their fundamental conduct is set forth first, followed by the retributions they must undergo.
For a thousand billion years, he was killed at every birth.
Because of this, he accumulated much enmity; he harmed sages and heroes, falsely seizing the innocent, and alienating the friendships of others.
Those who constantly delight in slandering and hating others will, upon death, enter the Black Rope Hell.
Those who employ many deceptions and take advantage of others, or who direct cruel and tyrannical punishments,
shall later be crushed by mountain-like machinery and pounded with iron pestles.
In their human lives they were fond of killing— horses, oxen, deer, sheep, swine, chickens, dogs,
and various insects— and they even crushed them with mountain-presses.
Out of delusion, greed, and cowardice, they would recklessly inflict poison and harm upon others.
Seeking wealth through unrighteous means, one’s body shall be crushed by an iron wheel.
Relying on power and teaching through force, one subdues those who are weak;
delighting in inflicting distress upon others, one is constantly trampled by elephants.
In this life, one who vexes their parents, or harasses śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas until they are filled with bitter resentment, will suffer the torment of burning in a future existence.
Or, one who strikes their parents, or those who are virtuous and devoted to the Path, [will likewise suffer].
And that which others ought to revere, one later undergoes boiling and treatment in hell.
Coercing others through intimidation to take what is not given, and falsely accusing innocent people,
one’s body is subsequently burned for a long time, crying out alone in agonizing groans.
Invading others to benefit oneself, receiving a trust and misappropriating it,
later burned within a fire-chamber, crying out for help with no one to save him;
calling what is not the Dharma "the Dharma," and calling what is the Dharma "not the Dharma."
Whoever slanders those who are not sages will later be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Though dwelling in the purity of a temple, if one commits transgressions and thus slanders the worthy, by this path one enters the deep hells.
Abandoning upright and wholesome deeds, one follows the path of evil and finds pleasure therein;
in a future life, one perishes within a latrine, feeding upon the worms of that latrine.
Setting fires to burn the grasslands and wilds, one thereby harms all manner of insects and creatures.
Later, one enters the prison of stacked firewood, where one is burned like a wild fire.
Those who were secretly treacherous yet appeared close and affectionate pierce one’s body with sharp blades;
iron-eared dogs and woodpeckers roll about together to devour the flesh.
If there are those who destroy the bridge of the Dharma, slander the one of supreme virtue,
they shall fall into hell and tread upon it, walking upon the path of sword-blades.
Those who violate another's wife shall have a massive body with a hundred feet.
Her appearance resembles that of a beautiful woman, yet her companion seizes her;
delighting in lewdness and casting her will loose upon another's wife,
she constantly encounters suffering, her body clinging to a thorny tree.
If, for the sake of various clever expedients, one kills insects born in water,
after killing them they fall into boiling water and are reborn within the River of Ashes.
Those who borrow and do not repay will have their bodies constantly pierced by iron hooks.
Heated iron blazes fiercely, and molten copper is poured down his throat.
Having harbored resentment and been filled with anger, and having dared to commit unrighteous acts, he rejoiced at the sight of others in distress;
for this, after death, he becomes a hell-guardian in the realm of Yama.
Having performed unwholesome deeds in life, one enters hell at death;
its pains are beyond counting, consisting entirely of suffering.
Thus has been fully explained the conduct of those born in the hells.
Hearing and understanding the affairs of animals, hungry ghosts, and spirits:
The body and mind each have three [unwholesome actions], and the four verbal ones constitute non-virtue;
With a restless and rapidly shifting mind, one falls into the realm of animals after death.
If one indulges excessively in lustful ways, one will later be reborn as a deluded insect—
such as a wild goose, a pigeon, a dove, a mandarin duck, a peacock, or even a flying moth.
Those who take pleasure in binding, beating, and whipping will suffer much affliction in future lives.
By one's own actions, one becomes an elephant, horse, or ox; through dying in anger, one becomes a snake.
Those who are arrogant and constantly disdain others are reborn as fierce beasts;
those who are contemptuous will, in future lives, become pigs, dogs, foxes, or donkeys.
Constantly harboring jealousy within, with a mind that never dwells in one place,
one will become a monkey in a future life, and with a coarse face,
become a bird. Greedy, stingy, and deceitful, such a person frequently commits acts of theft.
After death, one becomes a cat, a jackal, a tiger, a wolf, or a carnivorous beast.
Having practiced much giving yet harbored great anger, and having maintained a mind that was not upright,
one subsequently falls among the dragons, whereupon one possesses great supernormal powers.
Having practiced extensive giving with a mind full of anger, and treating others with contempt while being self-important,
one later becomes a kāla-baka bird, possessing great ferocity and power.
Though one’s own body enjoys sweet and delicious food, one gives what is foul to others.
After death, one becomes a foul-smelling hungry ghost, constantly eating worms within filth.
Delighting in harassing the elderly and children, as well as beggars and the sick,
one later becomes a stinking hungry ghost, consuming the impurities of childbirth and lactation.
Though they harbor stinginess and regret in their hearts, constantly fearing they will never have enough,
they later become black *preta*s who snatch food from below.
Claiming that giving brings no merit, they were never willing to give even a little.
Later one becomes a base hungry ghost, whose primary food is what people have vomited.
Not having given offerings while being pursued by slander, and eating coarse food while being self-exalting,
one later becomes a hungry ghost of the drains, constantly eating the coughs and spittle of others.
Not giving from what one possesses oneself, yet constantly hoping to seek from others,
one later becomes a destitute hungry ghost, unable to obtain what one desires.
Delighting in observing the faults of others, one treats people with the expectation of wealth.
In the future, one will become a wretched hungry ghost, whose primary food is the liver of the dead;
by using coarse speech to vex others and slandering people by speaking of their faults,
one will later become a parched hungry ghost, constantly swallowing fire and smoke.
Those who incite litigation, delight in quarreling, and are cruel and tyrannical, terrifying and distressing others,
will later become *jvālāmukha* (flame-mouthed) ghosts, feeding upon flying moths and insects.
Those who prohibit others from practicing giving and do not give even of their own accord, [shall likewise suffer].
Later, he becomes a large-bodied ghost with a mouth like a needle and a nose like a hair.
He hoards wealth to leave for his children, neither eating it himself nor giving it away;
when he dies, he belongs to the realm of Yama, and only when his children perform sacrifices does he obtain food.
Born as the head of a narrow pass, he oppressed others to pursue his own ends;
as a ghost, his form was hideously large, yet what he desired he never obtained.
His speech was constantly deceitful and mocking; he neither gave nor observed the precepts.
Indulging in pleasure with haste, one will ultimately be reborn among ghosts and spirits.
Using insects as bait, one hooks living beings for one’s own profit;
by killing and eating them, one becomes a malevolent spirit in future lives.
Giving with expectations for the future, lacking sincerity and prone to much anger,
one later becomes a *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost, with an exceedingly hideous countenance.
Being both wrathful and greedy, though fond of giving, one is addicted to wine.
One who delights in music, drumming, and dance becomes a guardian deity of the earth after death.
One who harbors no ill will and no envy toward kinsmen, both inside and outside the home,
later becomes a powerful deity who travels upon the clouds and winds.
One who gives houses, vehicles, and various delicious foods will find that wherever they go as a deity,
their dwellings follow them as they fly. Yet those who are fond of desires and indolent,
though they delight in giving flowers and incense, [do not attain such results].
Later, they become celestial musicians, sporting and acting according to their own hearts' desire.
Thus, the conduct of animals, hungry ghosts, and spirits has all been explained in summary;
furthermore, listen now to the causes of virtue.
As for the practices to be undertaken, there are also various categories;
since these applications are not of a single kind, I shall now explain them according to the facts.
For devas, humans, and asuras who seek long life—
Internally, one should reflect upon oneself: do not harm any living being.
If one does not exhaust others through lack of generosity, nor bind, beat, or harass them, but always brings peace to all sentient beings, then as a person one will be free from illness.
Not killing, he cherishes kindness and virtue; his mind remains firm and never wavers again.
He ultimately does no harm to any living being, and among men he is always benevolent and noble.
Though he has never offered even the slightest gift, he has received but a most minute amount in return.
Thereafter, the body suffers extreme pain; though one seeks little, one may not obtain it at all.
One who habitually takes the wealth of others and considers it an act of charity, though they later acquire riches, will swiftly lose them again.
One does not falsely seize what belongs to others, nor does one ever give anything away;
yet by constantly seeking through diligent toil, one obtains wealth passed down through generations.
Since one does not take the property of others, one always delights in practicing generosity oneself.
Having possessed wealth and riches for generations, one gains benefits that are exceedingly vast and wide.
If one naturally delights in observing the precepts and the fast, one will surely be wise in future lives;
by loving the Dharma, one attains renown and peace, becoming a worthy person with upright intent.
A son who serves his father well, And repeatedly offers sacrifices after he has passed away,
Also bestows respect upon the heavens, And thereafter obtains food wherever he goes.
One who delights in giving food Obtains life and a fine complexion in future births.
One will possess power, eloquence, and wealth; Free from illness, one shall always be at peace.
Those who delight in giving robes and coverings Shall lose their shamelessness and gain a beautiful countenance.
With a virtuous mind, they will be pleasing to behold; They will find joy and obtain all that they desire.
Those who give houses will find peaceful dwellings in future lives;
their palaces and all their residences shall be fully equipped with every requisite.
Those who provide wells and offer refreshing drinks for travelers shall enjoy bathing pools adorned with lotuses.
Whether one attains them or not in future lives, all that one desires is wealth.
One who practices generosity in this life by providing sandals, boats, carts, bridges, elephants, horses,
and various other vehicles, will obtain the celestial vehicle in future lives.
One who is free from anger is beloved by all; such a person is looked up to by everyone.
After death, they will be reborn as an eldest son of high station—this is the reward for one who has gifted orchards and trees.
Those who delight in giving servants and slaves, doing so with a mind of reverence, [attain this merit].
Later one obtains renown for one’s clan, with attendants and servants never lacking for anything.
Because the ancestors practiced great generosity, descendants continue the tradition without interruption;
later generations become immensely wealthy, immediately inheriting the surplus wealth left by their fathers.
One who delights in praising the virtue of giving, yet lacks the intention to actually bestow it,
will later fall among the ranks of humanity and be born into a poor and narrow household.
One who slanders giving as being of no benefit, yet gives only out of compassion, [will likewise suffer such consequences].
Though lacking the intent to give, one is still born into a family of wealth;
though the mind always delights in wisdom, yet not practicing giving,
one later always attains intelligence but is born into a destitute family.
If one always delights in giving but does not study wisdom,
one will lack proficiency in knowledge even if born into a great wealthy family.
If one practices both giving and wisdom, one will likewise receive the blessings of both.
If both [giving and receiving] are not practiced together, then neither will be attained.
Giving for the sake of reputation or fame, or giving as if one had already given when one has not,
or desiring to give later— these are the sufferings of being tormented by craving.
Although one may give without faith, one still obtains wealth and property;
if one delights in that giving of wealth, the mind will later feel great joy.
If one gives with faith, one will always possess abundant wealth in future lives.
Possessing much wealth enables one to attain honor, and the mind becomes exceedingly joyful.
By serving and respecting those of virtue, and by offering gifts with a benevolent heart,
one later obtains wealth to one's satisfaction, having attained that which is most excellent.
Always with a mind of ease and lightness, one bestows gifts upon those who cultivate virtue;
yet even if such a person subsequently acquires wealth, they will find no peace when times are difficult and obtain no food.
One who wishes to bring peace to others through giving does not act perversely or ensnare them.
Yet one gains what is loved and respected; among kinsmen, there are none who do not revere them.
Giving freely all that they possess, they cultivate virtue without contention;
later, they obtain what is beloved and joyful, fully endowed with the benefits of the Dharma.
One who gives with discerning eyes, Who does not flatter to seek what is not rightfully theirs,
Will have blessings passed down to their descendants, And their wealth preserved for generations.
When a wise person practices giving, They do not cause hardship for others when the time comes to use it.
Though young, do not lose the proper time; when enjoying the fruits of merit, let yourself be at ease.
Cultivate the self to maintain discipline, and do not take pleasure in violating another's wife.
Later, you will obtain what you love and desire: integrity, goodness, and the virtue of precepts.
When women act improperly, the wise man can sever himself from them;
later, he will have no cause for resentment and his nature will be profoundly pure.
If one cultivates pure conduct, his actions will be beyond reproach.
In future lives one will possess renown and be honored by the devas.
Having departed from drunkenness, practicing with constant purity,
one’s consciousness will not be deluded in the future, and one will gain the benefit of internal wisdom.
For the sake of oneself and others, one should never speak falsely;
in future lives, one will find comfort within one's own body, and no one shall speak of one's faults.
One should promptly reconcile friends who are at odds and take no pleasure in spreading false rumors.
In later life, one will not be separated from kin; the body will always be that of a hero among men.
Always speaking with gentle words, one’s loyalty reaches so deeply as to enter the hearts of others;
later, one’s speech will be skillful and agreeable to the multitude, such that none who hear it fail to love it.
When gathered in assembly for discussion, one speaks of matters according to the facts with moderation;
in future lives one attains eloquence and harmony, and people delight in listening when one speaks.
Regarding all that exists, the mind does not conceive of grasping it.
In future lives one’s mind will be at peace, never again harboring lingering anxieties.

Knowing that every action brings its own reflection, and that the retribution for manifold virtues is such that those who act as humans draw near to goodness, they shall enjoy a vast abundance of the fruits of their merit.
Constantly desiring to achieve benefit, hoping for renown and peace in the heavens, and knowing that birth is not eternal, one’s mind must surely contemplate the cultivation of virtue.
Good and evil truly reside in one's conduct; this is the great benefit for human relations.
Because the seeds are mixed, one reaps a mixed harvest; whether amidst the pure or the impure,
whether young, middle-aged, or old, when one acts with autonomy,
one subsequently receives at the proper time results that correspond to their original nature— be they suffering or joy.

Whether an action is brief or long-lasting, whatever one does—whether good or evil—if it is done moderately, one receives a moderate result; if it is done extensively, one receives an extensive result.
The words of loyal and considerate teachers and friends bring great benefit in both this life and the next.
Those who are negligent and refuse to accept or practice [the teachings] will, in future lives, always be deaf and mute.
Those who act with deceit and arrogance will, in future lives, be hunchbacked, short, and ugly;
they may be mute or have a hideous complexion, such that no clan or family wishes to see them.
One who does not attend to the elderly becomes foolish; one who serves those who possess the Way gains benefit.
One who does not treat the honorable with disrespect will remain noble, while arrogance leads to lowliness.
One who practices giving later becomes wealthy; one who lacks generosity becomes poor.
Through anger one obtains an ugly appearance; by not being angry, one later gains a beautiful appearance.
One who is fond of lewdness, whether male or female, and who desires to violate those who should not be violated, or who castrates various livestock, will be born in the future as a eunuch.
If one’s thoughts of lust are like a blazing fire, and one commits transgressions with body,
mind, and speech, single-mindedly seeking out women, one will be reborn as a eunuch in a future life.
When another speaks of the virtuous path of giving and comes to exhort one, if one joyfully follows their advice—
Viewing hatred and love with an equal mind, one will later possess the three eyes.
Rejoicing in giving fine garments to those of virtue,
one will always be refined and elegant in future lives, with a lustrous complexion like gold.
Regarding others as one's own infant, Protecting the elderly and the sick is likewise.
Later, he constantly encounters sages, As bright as the moon among the stars.
Not only does he observe the precepts of fasting, But also [protects] women in childbirth.
Later one obtains the joy of female attendants; the transgressor incurs slander.
By paying respect and showing universal love for the multitude, one later gains soft hands and palms.
Protecting wealth with stability and immovability, one receives honor like a great mountain.
Do not inquire after messengers or musicians; seek nothing but delight in giving.
Later, you will obtain food in abundance, and your accumulated wealth will be like the sea.
Possessing virtue, you will receive blessings from the heavens; through the goodness of the Dharma, the multitude will look up to you in reverence.
Later, noble and honored, he rejoices; born into the lineage of emperors and kings, his body and speech constantly practice goodness. He distributes gifts with a harmonious countenance;
later, though wealthy, none can envy him. Receiving joy, he is reborn in the northern region.
Repaying an enemy with kindness, never recklessly inflicting harm;
though contentious in speech, gentle in heart—one later becomes an asura.
If one perceives the path of goodness and possesses the capacity to see correctly, [one shall attain liberation].
Later one may be born in the heavens, shining like the light of the sun.
By serving one’s parents with filial piety, one will later be born into a noble family;
by not quarreling and not being prone to anger, one enjoys blessings in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
One does not engage in verbal disputes, nor does one participate in quarrels or litigation;
guarding a virtuous mind and cultivating merit, one will later be reborn in the radiant heavens.
Possessing much learning and dwelling in tranquil reflection, one values what is beneficial and seeks liberation.
Recalling virtuous deeds with goodness, one is reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Constantly guarding the precepts and practicing meditative reflection, relying on the Dharma without dependence on anything else,
and likewise encouraging others to do the same, one is reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Guarding oneself and delighting in supreme giving, not being contrary and not praising oneself,
impartial and loving those who possess the Way— one is born in that Nimmānarati Heaven.
Not inflicting the afflictions of whips, staves, or cords upon living beings, [one attains this state].
Comforting all people, one enjoys the blessings of the Brahma Heaven.
With a compassionate mind and virtuous speech, cherishing others as oneself,
and giving immediately to those who ask, one is born in that Kāyika Heaven.
Constantly mindful in conduct as one who observes the fast, Not desiring worldly delights, with a concentrated mind established in tranquility, One is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
With a concentrated mind, abandon attachment to women; Eliminate the three habits and find singular bliss.
One who can joyfully contemplate right stillness attains birth in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Regarding suffering and pleasure as impermanent, and knowing the movements of the body,
one who sees consciousness as most pure is born in the Vṛhatphala Heaven.
Thoroughly understanding the perception of impurity, one dwells much in the realm of the King of Existence;
having abandoned habitual tendencies and being without conceptualization, one is born in the Heaven of No-Perception.
Without reliance yet possessing subtle reliance, one expansively practices the four karmas.
Through mindfulness and dhyāna, one attains natural purity and concentration, And is born among the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
With a supple mind that is exceptionally sublime, A mind upright and a nature harmonious,
One extensively cultivates the karma of the heavens And is born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Understanding that form is impermanent, one delights in seeking boundless resolve;
when the consciousness of what is known is limitless, through contemplation one attains transcendence.
Having already departed from all sensory perceptions, there is no longer any direction toward which birth occurs.
Even when mindfulness has passed away, one may still desire to conceive of the non-conceptual;
though resolved, [defilements] arise again, and retribution manifests as parallel action.
The wise man observes for himself and knows that wholesome deeds should be performed.
This Dharma is uniquely sublime; therefore, it is fully explained for the sake of humanity.
It is not from gods, nor from time, nor from seeds; what one receives arises from one's own actions.
Birth is impermanent and should be observed; with wisdom, one should not harbor expectations or attachments.
All who are reborn in auspicious realms do so by relying on their conduct.
If one has realized that there is no self, then conditioned existence is empty;
by tranquil release, one extinguishes suffering and bitterness—this bliss is the most supreme.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Arising of the Distinction Between Good and Evil.
